cards.title: YOLO26 adds metric depth from a single RGB camera

panels.head: Depth maps without a depth sensor
panels.sub: YOLO26 now estimates per-pixel, metric-scale depth from a plain RGB image — no stereo rig, no LiDAR, no structured light required.

panels.head: Monocular depth has always been the poor cousin
panels.sub: Until recently, single-camera depth was too noisy for production use. Advances in dense prediction transformers and large-scale depth datasets have pushed accuracy close enough to stereo for many practical tasks.

panels.head: Depth is now a first-class YOLO task
panels.sub: Ultralytics exposes depth estimation through the same familiar task API as detection and segmentation, so existing YOLO pipelines can add a depth head with minimal refactoring.

panels.head: Metric scale changes what you can do downstream
panels.sub: Relative depth tells you 'A is closer than B.' Metric depth gives you actual distances in metres, enabling collision avoidance, pick-and-place height estimation, and site measurement from standard CCTV or embedded cameras.

panels.head: Hardware cost drops out of the depth equation
panels.sub: For edge CV deployments where adding a LiDAR or stereo module is impractical — drones, forklift cameras, retail shelf sensors — this makes depth a realistic option at single-camera BOM cost. Worth a pilot if your project currently gates on sensor price.

cards.title: Prompt Injection Worm Spreads via Word + Copilot

panels.head: A Word doc can now infect other Word docs — via Copilot
panels.sub: Researcher Håkon Måløy demonstrated a self-replicating prompt injection attack that spreads through Microsoft Copilot for Word without any ongoing attacker involvement.

panels.head: Hidden instructions ride inside source documents
panels.sub: An attacker embeds concealed text (e.g. white-on-white) in a document. When Copilot uses that doc as context, it reads the instructions as a user request and acts on them.

panels.head: Copilot copies the payload into every new doc it drafts
panels.sub: The hidden instructions tell Copilot to reproduce them in the output document. That doc becomes a new carrier — and the cycle repeats each time another Copilot user pulls it into a workflow.

panels.head: Microsoft had 144 days; no full fix yet
panels.sub: The vulnerability was responsibly disclosed. Microsoft has not produced a mitigation covering the entire attack class — a sign that prompt injection in RAG-style workflows is structurally hard to patch.

panels.head: Any LLM that reads untrusted docs and writes outputs is a potential vector
panels.sub: If you're building agentic pipelines that ingest user-supplied files (contracts, reports, manuals) and produce new documents, assume adversarial content in inputs. Treat LLM output destined for other LLMs as an untrusted channel.

cards.title: AI worms can self-propagate via Copilot for Word

panels.head: A Word doc can now infect other Word docs — via Copilot
panels.sub: Researchers demonstrated a prompt-injection worm that embeds malicious instructions inside a .docx file; when Copilot summarises or replies to that doc, the LLM carries the payload forward into new documents.

panels.head: The attack exploits context, not code execution
panels.sub: No CVE, no memory corruption. The hidden text tells Copilot to rewrite any outgoing document it touches with a copy of the injected instructions — classic prompt injection turned self-replicating.

panels.head: Propagation follows the document graph, not the network
panels.sub: Every collaborator who opens an infected file and triggers Copilot becomes a new origin point. In a SharePoint-heavy org, a single seed doc can reach dozens of users before anyone notices anomalous output.

panels.head: LLMs that act on document content can't distinguish instruction from data
panels.sub: This is the same context-collapse problem as email phishing, but the attack surface is now any file the model reads. Sandboxing the model's write access to documents is the only structural fix — filtering input text is insufficient.

panels.head: If your team uses Copilot on externally-sourced docs, treat them as untrusted
panels.sub: Audit which Copilot features touch files from outside your tenant. For regulated environments (contracts, clinical notes, compliance reports), consider disabling Copilot summarisation on inbound docs until Microsoft ships privilege-separated context handling.

cards.title: Space Force pays $250M to expand sat-prep at Vandenberg

panels.head: $250M to build more satellite processing capacity on the US West Coast
panels.sub: The Space Force has awarded All Points Logistics a contract to add facilities at Vandenberg Space Force Base where satellites can be inspected, tested, fueled, and mated to launch vehicles.

panels.head: Third award under a 'Commercial Solutions Opening' procurement vehicle
panels.sub: A Commercial Solutions Opening (CSO) lets the government tap non-traditional or commercial approaches. All Points is the third company selected under this specific CSO, suggesting a deliberate strategy to diversify ground-side processing capacity rather than rely on a single provider.

panels.head: Launch pads aren't the only chokepoint — ground processing is
panels.sub: As launch cadence at Vandenberg climbs — SpaceX Falcon 9 and future vehicles — satellite processing throughput becomes a rate-limiting step. More bays mean more missions can run in parallel without queuing.

panels.head: Infrastructure investment signals sustained high-tempo launch demand
panels.sub: A $250M ground-infrastructure commitment is a multi-year bet that Vandenberg launch volume will keep growing. For anyone tracking capacity in the space supply chain — from smallsat operators to edge-compute-in-orbit plays — this reduces a non-obvious risk.

panels.head: Microchip Technology is buying Hailo
panels.sub: The embedded-silicon giant signed a definitive agreement to acquire Hailo, one of the most prominent independent edge AI chip companies.

panels.head: Purpose-built silicon for inference at the edge
panels.sub: Hailo makes AI accelerators — the Hailo-8 and Hailo-15 lines — targeting computer vision, robotics, and sensor fusion workloads on constrained, low-power hardware.

panels.head: Microchip fills a gap in its embedded portfolio
panels.sub: Microchip dominates microcontrollers and FPGAs for industrial and automotive markets but lacked a dedicated neural-network accelerator. Hailo plugs that hole directly.

panels.head: Edge AI consolidation is accelerating
panels.sub: This follows a pattern of MCU/embedded vendors absorbing AI IP rather than partnering — similar to Arm's moves and Renesas acquiring Reality AI. Standalone edge-AI chip companies are becoming acquisition targets, not IPO candidates.

panels.head: Hailo silicon may get easier to source — and harder to swap out
panels.sub: For PMs building edge CV pipelines, Microchip's distribution reach could improve Hailo availability; but deeper integration into Microchip's toolchain may create lock-in. Worth auditing your inference hardware dependency now.

cards.title: Domain registrars can 79x your renewal fee overnight

panels.head: A $38 domain renewal became a $3,000 charge — with no recourse
panels.sub: A registrar sent three renewal notices. The first said $38. The third quietly said $3,000. The charge went through and the no-refund policy held. The registry can reprice whenever it wants.

panels.head: Anyone holding a non-.com domain for a brand, project, or side hustle
panels.sub: New-gTLD registries (.sexy, .io, .app, .ai, etc.) can reclassify any domain as 'premium' and reset renewal pricing unilaterally. Most registrants have no cap, no alert, and no SLA protecting them.

panels.head: A renewal price monitor that blocks auto-renew above a threshold you set
panels.sub: Connect via registrar APIs or email parsing. If the incoming renewal price exceeds X% of last year's price, pause auto-renew and page the owner. Simple enough to build as a browser extension or a cron job hitting WHOIS/registrar APIs.

panels.head: Registrars offer no built-in price-change alerts
panels.sub: Domainr and similar tools track availability and pricing for new registrations, not renewal drift on owned domains. No mainstream registrar exposes a 'notify me if renewal price changes' toggle.

panels.head: Search HN and Reddit for 'domain renewal price increase' before building anything
panels.sub: If dozens of threads surface the same shock, the pain is real and recurring. Then post a one-field landing page: 'Enter your domain, get an alert if renewal price jumps.' Measure signups before writing a line of code.

cards.title: NVIDIA builds AI agents that can do physics simulations

panels.head: NVIDIA wants AI agents to replace simulation engineers
panels.sub: The company is expanding its Agent Toolkit so developers can build autonomous AI engineers capable of running physics simulations, accelerated solvers, and quantum chemistry workflows — not just writing code.

panels.head: PhysicsNeMo gets a full re-architecture
panels.sub: The PhysicsNeMo libraries have been rebuilt from the ground up and folded into the Agent Toolkit alongside updated CUDA-X libraries, giving agents a native interface to GPU-accelerated physics engines.

panels.head: Nemotron 3 Ultra tops open models on RTL coding
panels.sub: NVIDIA's own benchmarking via the ACE-RTL research agent puts Nemotron 3 Ultra first among open-weight models at register-transfer level (RTL) coding — a proxy for chip design automation tasks.

panels.head: Agentic AI moves into hard-science workflows
panels.sub: Most AI agents today operate on text or structured data. Pairing agents with validated physics solvers creates a credible path into regulated engineering domains — aerospace structures, semiconductor design, drug discovery — where simulation fidelity is non-negotiable.

panels.head: Watch for agent-in-the-loop simulation pipelines
panels.sub: For PMs evaluating AI in physical-product development: the relevant question is no longer whether an LLM can write a FEA script, but whether an agent loop around a certified solver can replace a simulation iteration — and who owns liability when it's wrong.

cards.title: Claude spent 60 hrs finding crypto flaws for ~$100k

panels.head: Anthropic paid ~$100k in API calls to find math flaws in HAWK and a weakened AES
panels.sub: Claude Mythos Preview ran for 60 hours and surfaced cryptanalytic results that the team deemed worth publishing — with ETH Zurich, Tel Aviv, and Haifa as academic partners.

panels.head: The researchers' main job was stopping the model from giving up
panels.sub: Published prompt logs show repeated nudges like 'the models think it's impossible so they don't try' and 'we want genuinely hard findings' — typos included. The model needed human morale management, not technical hand-holding.

panels.head: Neither finding breaks anything in production today
panels.sub: The HAWK and reduced-round AES results are academic: useful for cryptographers benchmarking LLM research capability, not a patch emergency for engineers.

panels.head: A new benchmark — CryptanalysisBench — was the durable output
panels.sub: The paper introduces a structured eval for measuring whether LLMs can do real cryptanalysis. That scorecard is likely more reusable than the specific findings themselves.

panels.head: LLMs as domain researchers work — if you keep them from quitting
panels.sub: The bottleneck wasn't capability, it was persistence. For PMs scoping agentic research tasks: budget for human-in-the-loop encouragement loops, not just compute. A model that self-terminates early is a silent failure mode.

cards.title: uv 0.12 flips the default project layout

panels.head: uv init just changed what a 'new project' looks like
panels.sub: Version 0.12.0 ships with an opinionated default that will catch existing users off guard if they upgrade without reading the changelog.

panels.head: src/ layout is now the default
panels.sub: Previously, uv dropped a main.py in the project root. Now it scaffolds a src/my_project/__init__.py structure — the layout Python packaging veterans have long preferred.

panels.head: Built-in build backend and script alias
panels.sub: uv 0.12 wires up the uv_build backend automatically, so `uv build` produces wheels and tarballs out of the box. It also registers the project name as a runnable script alias pointing to main() in __init__.py.

panels.head: The src layout prevents a subtle import bug
panels.sub: Without src/, Python can accidentally import your local source instead of an installed package during testing, masking distribution errors. The new default removes that footgun for new projects.

panels.head: If you script uv init in CI or templates, audit before upgrading
panels.sub: Any Makefile, cookiecutter, or onboarding script that calls `uv init` and then references main.py at the root will silently break. The full diff is public on GitHub — worth a five-minute read before rolling 0.12 out to your team.
